analysis.evidence: Abram asks Sarai to say the words אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ, “You are my sister.” The separate particle נָא adds “please” to the request.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperative, second person feminine singular. The ending ־ִי marks the feminine singular addressee.

analysis.evidence: נָא follows אִמְרִי, the feminine singular imperative “say.” Abram asks Sarai, “Please say you are my sister.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew particle of entreaty with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Abram asks Sarai to say אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ, “you are my sister.” The suffix refers to Abram, and אָתְּ identifies Sarai as the sister in the claim.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state with a first-person singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ, “you are my sister,” אָתְּ is the subject and אֲחֹתִי gives the relationship Abram asks Sarai to claim.
analysis.morphology: Independent second-person feminine singular pronoun in its pausal form.
analysis.sense: you (are): the woman addressed named or identified

analysis.evidence: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister. לְמַעַן introduces the outcome he hopes for in יִיטַב לִי בַעֲבוּרֵךְ, “that it may go well for me because of you.”
analysis.morphology: The fixed form לְמַעַן is tagged as a single preposition. Before the imperfect יִיטַב it functions as a purpose conjunction.

analysis.evidence: In לְמַעַן יִיטַב לִי בַעֲבוּרֵךְ, “so that it may go well with me on your account,” לִי identifies Abram as the one who hopes to benefit. The following clause specifies the outcome he hopes for, that his life will be spared.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, third person masculine singular, used impersonally in a purpose clause introduced by לְמַעַן.
